chapters.title: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read (with poem: Bharat Our Land)

topics.title: Sudha Murty's story: reading a first-person narrative

learn.hook: Can a granddaughter become her grandmother's teacher? This lesson says yes, and it is told by the girl herself!
points: Sudha Murty is an Indian author who writes in both English and Kannada. In this lesson she recalls, in her own voice, teaching her grandmother to read.
A first-person narrative is told by a narrator who uses 'I' and 'me', so we see events through that person's eyes and feelings.
Every story has characters, a setting (time and place), a problem or conflict, and a resolution. The theme is the big idea the story leaves with us.
Stories about the past mostly use the simple past (she wrote). The past perfect (she had written) shows an action that happened before another past action.
Good readers infer: they use clues such as actions and descriptions to understand feelings that the writer does not state directly.

example.q: Read this short passage (our own): 'Every evening Ajji sat on the swing with a slate on her lap. Her fingers, used to rolling rotis, now traced the curly letters of Kannada. When she finally read the name on the bus board aloud, she laughed like a child who had found a hidden sweet.' How does Ajji feel at the end, and which words show it?
steps: Look at what Ajji does at the end: she reads the bus board aloud and laughs.
Look at the comparison: 'like a child who had found a hidden sweet' suggests surprise and delight.
Put the clues together to name the feeling.
example.answer: She feels joyful and proud; the words 'laughed like a child who had found a hidden sweet' show it.

learn.reallife: When you help a younger cousin read a signboard or teach a grandparent to use a phone, you are living this story's theme.

games.title: Match the story elements
pairs: The voice that tells the story
The time and place of the story
The central message of the story

games.title: Put the mini-story in order
games.prompt: Arrange the events of this short story from first to last
items: Ajji says she wishes she could read the temple notice board.
Her granddaughter offers to teach her every evening.
Ajji practises letters on a slate for many weeks.
Ajji reads the notice board aloud by herself.
The whole family claps and Ajji smiles proudly.

quiz.q: 'I watched my grandmother press her thumb on the ink pad, her eyes lowered.' From which point of view is this sentence told?
quiz.explain: The narrator uses 'I', so the sentence is told in the first person.
steps: Point of view depends on the pronoun the narrator uses.
The narrator says 'I watched…', so the narrator is inside the story.
'I/me' narration is first person.
Answer: First person
quiz.mistake: Thinks that a sentence about another person (the grandmother) must be third person

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the past perfect tense correctly?
options: She has learnt the letters before the festival began.
She had learnt the letters before the festival began.
She had learn the letters before the festival began.
She learnt had the letters before the festival began.
quiz.explain: The past perfect is had + past participle (had learnt). It shows the learning was finished before another past action (the festival began).
steps: Past perfect = had + past participle, for the earlier of two past actions.
'had learnt' is correct; 'has learnt' is present perfect and 'had learn' uses the wrong form.
Answer: She had learnt the letters before the festival began.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the present perfect (has learnt) with the past perfect, or uses the base form after 'had'

quiz.q: In a story, what does the 'setting' mean?
options: The time and place where the story happens
The last line of the story
quiz.explain: The setting tells us when and where events take place.
steps: Setting = the time and place of a story.
Names, lessons and last lines are other story elements.
Answer: The time and place where the story happens
quiz.mistake: Mixes up setting with theme or character

quiz.q: Read: 'Rehana's grandfather hid the letter behind his back whenever the postman came, then quietly asked the neighbour's boy to read it to him.' What can you infer?
options: He is angry with the postman
He does not love his family
He wants to become a postman
He cannot read and feels shy about it
quiz.explain: Asking someone else to read the letter and hiding it suggests he cannot read and is embarrassed about it.
steps: Clues: he hides the letter and asks a boy to read it quietly.
Hiding and asking quietly suggest he cannot read and feels embarrassed.
Nothing shows anger or lack of love.
Answer: He cannot read and feels shy about it
quiz.mistake: Picks a feeling that has no clue in the passage

quiz.q: Which word best describes a learner who keeps trying even when lessons are hard?
quiz.explain: 'Determined' means firmly deciding to do something and not giving up.
steps: The learner keeps trying when lessons are hard.
'Determined' means firmly deciding not to give up.
Answer: Determined
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of 'determined'

quiz.q: Which statement best describes the theme of a story?
options: The number of pages in it
The central idea or message it shares
quiz.explain: The theme is the main idea or insight about life that the story conveys.
steps: Theme = the central idea or message a story leaves with us.
Page counts, publishers and character lists are not themes.
Answer: The central idea or message it shares
quiz.mistake: Thinks theme means a plain fact about the book

quiz.q: In which languages does Sudha Murty write?
quiz.explain: Sudha Murty writes in both English and Kannada, the language of Karnataka.
steps: Sudha Murty writes in English and in Kannada, the language of Karnataka.
Answer: English and Kannada
quiz.mistake: Guesses a language without linking the author to Karnataka

quiz.q: Choose the correct verb: 'Yesterday, Ajji ___ her name for the first time.'
quiz.explain: 'Yesterday' points to a finished past time, so we use the simple past 'wrote'.
steps: 'Yesterday' marks a finished past time.
A finished past action takes the simple past.
'has written' cannot be used with 'yesterday'.
Answer: wrote
quiz.mistake: Uses the present perfect with a finished past time word like 'yesterday'

teach.ask: Gappu flutters over: "Who is telling this story, and what is a theme? I keep forgetting!"
teach.praise: Tweet! The narrator tells it in first person, and the theme is the big message. I get it now!
teach.nudge: Okay, but who tells the story, and what is the message it leaves us with?

revise.summary: In 'How I Taught My Grandmother to Read', Sudha Murty recalls in the first person teaching her grandmother to read. Readers identify story elements, use the simple past and past perfect, and infer feelings from clues.
focus: First-person narration and point of view
Story elements: characters, setting, conflict, resolution, theme
Inferring feelings from actions and descriptions
remember: First person = narrator uses 'I' and 'me'
Setting = time and place; theme = central idea or message
Past perfect = had + past participle, for the earlier of two past actions
Sudha Murty writes in English and Kannada
traps: Don't use the present perfect with a finished past time like 'yesterday'.
Don't write 'had learn'; the past perfect needs the past participle.

topics.title: Learning at any age: literacy words and modals

learn.hook: Your nani learnt to use video calls, didn't she? Learning has no birthday limit!
points: Literacy is the ability to read and write. A literate person can read and write; an illiterate person cannot yet do so.
Words like literacy, literate, literal and literature belong to one word family. They come from the Latin word 'littera', meaning a letter of the alphabet.

Negative prefixes change a word to its opposite: il- before many words starting with l (illiterate, illegal), im- before many words starting with m or p (immature, impossible), ir- before many words starting with r (irregular).
Modals add meaning to verbs: can (present ability), could (past ability or a polite request), may (permission or possibility), must (necessity or a rule), should (advice).
Lifelong learning means continuing to learn throughout life, at any age.

example.q: Fill in the modals: 'Last year Dadaji ___ not sign his name, but now he ___ write a whole letter.'
steps: The first blank is about the past (last year) and ability, so we need the past form of 'can'.
The second blank is about ability now, so we need 'can'.
example.answer: could, can

learn.reallife: International Literacy Day is observed every year on 8 September. Many villages and towns run evening classes where adults learn to read and write.

items.text: You ___ wear a helmet on a two-wheeler; it is the law.
___ I borrow your pencil, please?
You look tired; you ___ rest for a while.
When she was five, Meera ___ swim across the pond.

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'literate'?
quiz.explain: Words beginning with 'l' often take the prefix il-, so literate becomes illiterate.
steps: Negative prefix il- goes before many words starting with l.
literate → illiterate
Answer: illiterate
quiz.mistake: Adds a common prefix like un- without checking which prefix the word takes

quiz.q: Which word does NOT come from the Latin 'littera' (letter)?
quiz.explain: 'Liberty' comes from a different Latin word meaning free; the others are linked to letters.
steps: literacy, literate, literal and literature come from Latin 'littera' (a letter).
'Liberty' comes from a Latin word meaning free.
Answer: liberty
quiz.mistake: Groups words only because they look alike at the start

quiz.q: What does 'lifelong' mean in 'lifelong learning'?
quiz.explain: 'Lifelong' means continuing for the whole of a person's life.
steps: 'Lifelong' = lasting the whole of one's life.
Lifelong learning means learning at any age.
Answer: Lasting throughout one's life
quiz.mistake: Thinks learning belongs only to school years

quiz.q: 'You should read for twenty minutes every day.' What does 'should' express here?
quiz.explain: 'Should' is used to give advice or a suggestion.
steps: Modals: can = ability, may = permission, must = necessity, should = advice.
'You should read…' is a suggestion.
Answer: Advice
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'should' (advice) with 'must' (strong necessity)

quiz.q: Read: 'At sixty-five, Kamla Bai joined the evening class at the panchayat hall. At first her hand shook as she held the chalk. By Diwali she could write the names of all her grandchildren.' What change happened in Kamla Bai?
options: She became the teacher of the class
She stopped going to the class
She moved to a new village
quiz.explain: The passage says that by Diwali she could write her grandchildren's names, so she learnt to write.
steps: At first her hand shook holding the chalk.
By Diwali she could write her grandchildren's names.
So the change is that she learnt to write.
Answer: She learnt to write
quiz.mistake: Picks a detail that the passage does not mention

quiz.q: Which prefix makes the opposite of 'responsible'?
quiz.explain: Many words beginning with 'r' take ir-, giving 'irresponsible'.
steps: ir- goes before many words starting with r.
responsible → irresponsible
Answer: ir-
quiz.mistake: Uses un- for every opposite

quiz.q: In which sentence does 'could' show past ability?
options: Could you pass the salt, please?
As a girl, Nani could climb the mango tree in seconds.
quiz.explain: 'As a girl' places the action in the past, and 'could' tells what she was able to do then.
steps: 'Could' can show past ability, a polite request or possibility.
'As a girl' places the action in the past and tells what she was able to do.
The others are a request, a possibility and a suggestion.
Answer: As a girl, Nani could climb the mango tree in seconds.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that 'could' also makes polite requests, possibilities and suggestions

quiz.q: Which saying best matches the idea that learning has no age limit?
options: It is never too late to learn.
Too many cooks spoil the broth.
quiz.explain: 'It is never too late to learn' says anyone can start learning at any age.
steps: The idea: learning has no age limit.
'It is never too late to learn' says anyone can start at any age.
Answer: It is never too late to learn.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a familiar proverb without matching its meaning

teach.ask: Gappu sighs: "My grandpa says he is too old to learn to read. What does literate mean, and is he really too old?"
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Literate means able to read and write, and nobody is ever too old to learn. I'll tell Grandpa!
teach.nudge: But what exactly can a literate person do, and does age stop anyone from learning?

revise.summary: Literacy is the ability to read and write, and words like literate and literature come from Latin 'littera'. Negative prefixes il-, im- and ir- form opposites, and modals add shades of meaning. Learning can continue at any age.
focus: Meanings of modals can, could, may, must, should
Reading short passages about adult learners
remember: literate → illiterate; legal → illegal; possible → impossible; regular → irregular; responsible → irresponsible
can = present ability; could = past ability or polite request
may = permission or possibility; must = necessity; should = advice
Lifelong learning = learning throughout life
traps: Not every 'lit-/lib-' word is in the family: liberty comes from a word meaning free.
'Could you pass the salt?' is a polite request, not past ability.

topics.title: Poem on India's land: imagery and poetic devices

learn.hook: Can a few lines of poetry fit the Himalayas, the sea and the desert all at once? Poets do it with clever word-pictures!
points: The lesson pairs the story with a poem on the theme of India's land. Poems like this often picture mountains, rivers, fields and seas.
Imagery is language that appeals to the senses: sight, sound, smell, taste or touch.
Personification gives human actions or feelings to non-human things, such as 'the river sings'.
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor says one thing IS another. Alliteration repeats the same beginning consonant sound in nearby words.
The rhyme scheme is the pattern of rhyming line endings, marked with letters such as aabb or abab.

example.q:
Read this original poem:
'From Himalayan peaks of snow
To southern seas where warm winds blow,
The Ganga hums a silver tune,
Thar's golden dunes sleep under the moon;
Green paddy dances in the rain,
One land, with colours none can contain.'
What is the rhyme scheme, and find one example of personification.
steps: Mark the end words: snow, blow (a a); tune, moon (b b); rain, contain (c c).
Look for non-human things doing human actions: the Ganga hums, the dunes sleep, the paddy dances.
example.answer: The rhyme scheme is aabbcc; 'The Ganga hums a silver tune' is personification (so are 'dunes sleep' and 'paddy dances').

learn.reallife: Patriotic songs sung on Republic Day and Independence Day are full of imagery of rivers, mountains and fields.

games.title: Match the device to its example
pairs: The river shines like a silver ribbon
India is a garden of many flowers
The monsoon knocks on our windows

games.title: True or false?
items: In 'The Ganga hums a silver tune', the river is personified.
Humming is a human action given to a river.
A simile compares two things without using 'like' or 'as'.
That describes a metaphor; a simile uses 'like' or 'as'.
Imagery can appeal to smell and sound, not only to sight.
Imagery can appeal to any of the five senses.
'warm winds' is an example of alliteration.
Both words begin with the same 'w' sound.
In a rhyme scheme, lines that rhyme with each other get different letters.
Rhyming lines get the same letter, for example 'a' and 'a'.
The Thar Desert lies in western India, mostly in Rajasthan.
The Thar, or Great Indian Desert, covers much of western Rajasthan.

quiz.q: 'Thar's golden dunes sleep under the moon.' Which device is used here?
quiz.explain: Sand dunes cannot sleep; giving them a human action is personification.
steps: Dunes cannot really sleep.
Giving a human action to a non-human thing is personification.
Answer: Personification
quiz.mistake: Sees a description of nature and calls it a simile even though 'like' or 'as' is missing

quiz.q: What is the rhyme scheme of these lines? 'The mountains stand so proud and tall, / They guard the land, they watch us all. / The rivers run to meet the sea, / And sing of home to you and me.'
quiz.explain: tall/all rhyme (aa) and sea/me rhyme (bb), giving aabb.
steps: Line endings: tall (a), all (a), sea (b), me (b).
Pattern: aabb.
Answer: aabb
quiz.mistake: Gives a new letter to every line without checking which endings rhyme

quiz.q: Which line contains a simile?
options: The diya smiled at the dark.
Life is a festival of lights.
Her smile was as bright as a diya.
quiz.explain: It compares her smile to a diya using 'as ... as', which makes it a simile.
steps: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'.
'as bright as a diya' compares her smile to a diya.
'Life is a festival of lights' is a metaphor.
Answer: Her smile was as bright as a diya.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a metaphor or personification with a simile

quiz.q: 'The smell of wet earth after the first rain' appeals mainly to which sense?
quiz.explain: The word 'smell' tells us the image appeals to the sense of smell.
steps: Imagery appeals to a sense.
The image is about the smell of wet earth.
Answer: Smell
quiz.mistake: Assumes all imagery is visual

quiz.q: 'India is a necklace of many bright beads.' Which device is this?
quiz.explain: It says India IS a necklace, without 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor.
steps: A metaphor says one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as'.
'India is a necklace…' does exactly this.
Answer: Metaphor
quiz.mistake: Calls every comparison a simile

quiz.q: Which word describes the Himalayas most vividly in a poem?
quiz.explain: 'Majestic' means grand and impressive, which suits huge snowy mountains.
steps: The Himalayas are huge, snowy mountains.
'Majestic' means grand and impressive; tiny, shallow, flat do not fit.
Answer: Majestic
quiz.mistake: Chooses a word whose meaning does not fit mountains

quiz.q: What does 'diverse' mean in 'India is a diverse land'?
quiz.explain: 'Diverse' means varied, with many different kinds of people, places and cultures.
steps: 'Diverse' means varied.
A diverse land has many different kinds of people, places and cultures.
Answer: Having many different kinds
quiz.mistake: Guesses the meaning without using the context

quiz.q: Which pair of words rhymes?
quiz.explain: 'Tune' and 'moon' end with the same 'oon' sound.
steps: Rhyming words end with the same sound.
'Tune' and 'moon' both end with 'oon'.
Answer: tune – moon
quiz.mistake: Thinks words starting with the same letter rhyme

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do poets make mountains and rivers come alive in a poem?"
teach.praise: Wow! Imagery, personification and comparisons turn a map into a living picture!
teach.nudge: Hmm, but which tricks make the river seem alive or help me picture it?

revise.summary: The lesson's poem pictures India's land. Poets use imagery, personification, simile, metaphor and alliteration, and line endings follow a rhyme scheme like aabb or abab.
focus: Imagery and the sense it appeals to
remember: Imagery appeals to sight, sound, smell, taste or touch
Personification gives human actions to non-human things
Simile uses 'like' or 'as'; metaphor says one thing IS another
Rhyme scheme is marked with letters: aabb, abab
traps: A comparison without 'like' or 'as' is a metaphor, not a simile.
Words that look alike (tune–tone) do not necessarily rhyme.

chapters.title: The Pot Maker (with poem: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations)

topics.title: Craft and pottery: words from the potter's wheel

learn.hook: A lump of mud, a spinning wheel and two patient hands: in minutes you have a diya! How does that magic happen?
points: The lesson 'The Pot Maker' is about the craft of pottery and the skill of the person who shapes clay.
Pottery is the craft of making pots and other objects from clay. A potter shapes wet clay on a spinning wheel, called a chaak in Hindi.
Key words: kiln (a very hot oven for firing clay), terracotta (baked clay; the Italian words mean 'baked earth'), glaze (a glassy coating), kulhad (a clay cup), matka (a clay water pot).
Clay is kneaded to make it smooth and to push out air bubbles, which could make a pot crack when it is fired.
To describe a process, we often use the passive voice: is/are + past participle, as in 'The clay is kneaded.' The action matters more than who does it.

example.q: Change into the passive voice: 'The potter fires the pots in a kiln.'
steps: Find the object of the active sentence: 'the pots'. It becomes the subject.
The verb 'fires' is in the simple present, so use are + past participle: 'are fired'.
Add 'by the potter' only if the doer is important.
example.answer: The pots are fired in a kiln (by the potter).

learn.reallife: Kulhad chai at a railway station, matkas sold in summer and terracotta diyas at Diwali all come from a potter's wheel.

games.title: How a clay pot is made
games.prompt: Put the steps of making a pot in order
items: Knead the clay to remove air bubbles
Shape the pot on the spinning wheel
Fire the pot in a kiln

games.title: Potter's word bank
pairs: A very hot oven for firing clay
A small clay cup for tea

quiz.q: What is a kiln?
options: A very hot oven used to fire clay objects
quiz.explain: A kiln is an oven or furnace that heats clay to a high temperature so that it hardens.
steps: A kiln is a very hot oven or furnace.
It fires clay so that it hardens.
Answer: A very hot oven used to fire clay objects
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the kiln with the clay or the potter's tools

quiz.q: What does the word 'terracotta' literally mean?
quiz.explain: 'Terracotta' comes from Italian words meaning 'baked earth'.
steps: 'Terracotta' comes from Italian words.
They mean 'baked earth'.
Answer: Baked earth
quiz.mistake: Guesses from the reddish colour instead of the word's origin

quiz.q: Which is the correct passive form of 'The potter shapes the clay'?
options: The clay is shaping by the potter.
The clay is shaped by the potter.
The potter is shaped by the clay.
quiz.explain: The object 'the clay' becomes the subject, and the simple present passive is is + past participle (is shaped).
steps: Passive: the object becomes the subject, verb = is/are + past participle.
'the clay' → subject; 'shapes' → 'is shaped'.
'is shaping' is active continuous, not passive.
Answer: The clay is shaped by the potter.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the doer and the receiver, or uses the -ing form instead of the past participle

quiz.q: Why does a potter knead the clay before shaping it?
options: To make it wet and sticky forever
To make it smooth and push out air bubbles
quiz.explain: Kneading makes the clay even and removes trapped air that could cause cracks in the kiln.
steps: Kneading makes clay smooth.
It pushes out air bubbles that could crack the pot in the kiln.
Answer: To make it smooth and push out air bubbles
quiz.mistake: Thinks kneading is only for colour or smell

quiz.q: Read: 'In Ramu Kaka's courtyard the wheel spun with a soft whirr. A lump of grey clay rose between his palms, and in a minute it had become a little lamp. "Clay listens to patient hands," he smiled.' What does Ramu Kaka mean?
options: Good work in clay needs patience
Only old people can make pots
quiz.explain: He means clay takes a good shape only when the potter works calmly and patiently.
steps: Clay cannot literally listen.
He means it takes a good shape only with calm, patient work.
Answer: Good work in clay needs patience
quiz.mistake: Reads the figurative line literally

quiz.q: 'A lump of clay rose between his palms like a growing bud.' Which device is used?
quiz.explain: The clay is compared to a bud using 'like', so it is a simile.
steps: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'.
The clay is compared to a bud using 'like'.
Answer: Simile
quiz.mistake: Calls every comparison a metaphor

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
options: Diyas are made in large numbers before Diwali.
My sister paints diyas every year.
We light diyas on Diwali night.
quiz.explain: 'Are made' is be + past participle, and the subject (diyas) receives the action.
steps: Passive = be + past participle, with the subject receiving the action.
'Diyas are made…' fits; the others are active.
Answer: Diyas are made in large numbers before Diwali.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence about making things is passive

quiz.q: Why does water in a clay matka stay cool in summer?
options: Water seeps through tiny pores and evaporates, cooling the pot
The matka is kept near a fire
quiz.explain: A matka has tiny pores; water slowly seeps out and evaporates from the surface, and evaporation cools the pot and the water.
steps: A matka has tiny pores.
Water seeps out and evaporates from the surface.
Evaporation takes away heat, so the water stays cool.
Answer: Water seeps through tiny pores and evaporates, cooling the pot
quiz.mistake: Does not connect evaporation with cooling

teach.ask: Gappu peeks at a matka: "How does wet mud become a hard pot, and what words describe it?"
teach.praise: Whirr! Clay on the wheel, then fired in the kiln. I could almost be a potter!
teach.nudge: But how does the soft clay become hard? What happens to it at the end?

revise.summary: 'The Pot Maker' is about pottery and the potter's skill. Key words include kiln, terracotta, glaze, kulhad and matka, and processes are often described in the passive voice.
focus: Why clay is kneaded and fired
Inference and devices in short craft passages
remember: Kiln = very hot oven for firing clay; terracotta = 'baked earth'
Chaak = potter's wheel; glaze = glassy coating
Kneading removes air bubbles that could crack a pot
Passive: The clay is shaped (by the potter).
traps: 'The clay is shaping' is not passive; use 'is shaped'.
A matka cools water by evaporation, not because of ice or paint.

topics.title: Dignity of work: respecting every vocation

learn.hook: Who keeps your school clean, your clothes stitched and your shoes mended? Every one of them is a hero of everyday life!
points: Dignity of labour means that every kind of honest work deserves respect, whether it is done with the hands or with a pen.
Useful words: vocation (work a person feels suited to or called to do), artisan (a skilled craftsperson), livelihood (the way a person earns a living), toil (hard work).
Many job names are made by adding a suffix to a verb or noun: weave + er = weaver, sculpt + or = sculptor, art + ist = artist, electric + ian = electrician.
Subject-verb agreement: a singular subject takes a singular verb (The weaver works); two subjects joined by 'and' usually take a plural verb (The potter and his son work).
Words like each, every, everyone and nobody take a singular verb. With 'either ... or' and 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it.

example.q: Choose the correct verb: 'Every craftsperson in the village (take / takes) pride in good work.'
steps: The subject begins with 'Every', which makes it singular.
A singular subject in the simple present takes the -s form of the verb.
example.answer: takes

learn.reallife: On Labour Day (1 May) and on days like Teachers' Day, many schools thank the helpers, guards, cooks and cleaners who keep the school running.

games.title: Is or are?
items: The weaver and the dyer ___ friends.
The potter's tools ___ on the shelf.
Neither the potter nor his sons ___ at home.
Neither the sons nor the potter ___ at home.

games.title: Who does what?
pairs: Shapes iron by heating and hammering

quiz.q: What does 'dignity of labour' mean?
options: Every kind of honest work deserves respect
quiz.explain: Dignity of labour is the idea that all honest work, of hand or mind, is worthy of respect.
steps: Dignity of labour = all honest work deserves respect.
It includes work of the hand and of the mind.
Answer: Every kind of honest work deserves respect
quiz.mistake: Thinks respect depends on the type of job or the salary

quiz.q: What does 'livelihood' mean?
options: The way a person earns a living
quiz.explain: Livelihood is the means by which a person earns money to live.
steps: 'Livelihood' = the way a person earns a living.
Answer: The way a person earns a living
quiz.mistake: Splits the word into 'live' and 'hood' and guesses

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'artisan'?
quiz.explain: An artisan is a skilled worker who makes things by hand, that is, a craftsperson.
steps: An artisan is a skilled worker who makes things by hand.
That is a craftsperson.
Answer: Craftsperson
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'artisan' with 'artist' in a general sense, or picks a random person

quiz.q: Choose the correct verb: 'The potter and his daughter ___ pots at the fair every Sunday.'
quiz.explain: Two subjects joined by 'and' make a plural subject, so the verb is 'sell'.
steps: Two subjects joined by 'and' make a plural subject.
Plural subject → plural verb 'sell'; 'every Sunday' needs the simple present.
Answer: sell
quiz.mistake: Looks only at the nearest noun 'daughter' and uses a singular verb

quiz.q: Choose the correct verb: 'Neither the baskets nor the mat ___ ready yet.'
quiz.explain: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'the mat', which is singular.
steps: With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
The nearer subject is 'the mat' (singular).
Answer: is
quiz.mistake: Treats 'neither ... nor' like 'and' and uses a plural verb

quiz.q: Which is the correct word for a person who sculpts?
quiz.explain: The job name is 'sculptor', with the suffix -or.
steps: sculpt + -or gives the job name.
Answer: Sculptor
quiz.mistake: Adds the most common suffix -er without checking the spelling

quiz.q: Read: 'Lakshmi Didi sweeps the school corridor before the first bell. When Arjun dropped his lunch, she helped him clean up with a smile. On Teachers' Day the class gave her a card that said, "Our school shines because of you."' What does the card show?
options: The class is angry with her
The class wants her to leave
The class thinks her work is unimportant
The class respects and values her work
quiz.explain: The card thanks her and says the school shines because of her, which shows respect and gratitude.
steps: The card says 'Our school shines because of you.'
It thanks her and values her work.
Answer: The class respects and values her work
quiz.mistake: Misses the positive meaning of 'shines because of you'

quiz.q: What is the antonym of 'respect'?
quiz.explain: Adding dis- gives the opposite meaning: disrespect.
steps: Antonym = opposite meaning.
Adding dis- to respect gives disrespect; honour, regard, admire are synonyms.
Answer: Disrespect
quiz.mistake: Picks a synonym instead of an antonym

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Is a cobbler's work less important than a doctor's? And why do we say 'Everyone works' and not 'Everyone work'?"
teach.praise: Chirp! Every honest job deserves respect, and 'everyone' is singular, so it takes 'works'. Grammar and kindness together!
teach.nudge: Hmm, should we respect only some jobs? And is 'everyone' singular or plural?

revise.summary: Dignity of labour means every kind of honest work deserves respect. The lesson builds vocation vocabulary, job-name suffixes and rules of subject-verb agreement.
remember: Livelihood = the way a person earns a living; artisan = craftsperson
weaver, sculptor, artist, electrician
A and B → plural verb; each/every/everyone/nobody → singular verb
Either…or / neither…nor → verb agrees with the nearer subject
traps: It is 'sculptor', not 'sculpter'.
'Neither the baskets nor the mat is…' — the verb follows 'the mat'.

topics.title: Gifts of Grace: reading a poem about vocations

learn.hook: The bread you eat, the shirt you wear, the book you read: count how many workers' gifts reach you before breakfast!
points: The poem in this lesson honours different vocations and the gifts each one brings to society.
The central idea of a poem is its main message, which can be said in one or two sentences.
Tone is the poet's attitude, such as grateful, joyful, sad or angry. Word choice shows the tone.
Anaphora is the repetition of the same word or words at the start of nearby lines, used for emphasis and rhythm.
A couplet is a pair of lines, usually rhyming; a quatrain is a stanza of four lines.

example.q:
Read this original poem:
'The farmer gives the bread we break,
The weaver weaves the clothes we wear,
The teacher lights the minds awake,
The nurse brings comfort, calm and care.
No work is small, no hand is low;
Each gift of grace helps all to grow.'
What is the central idea and the tone?
steps: Notice the list of workers and what each one gives us.
The last couplet sums it up: no work is small.
Words like 'gives', 'gift' and 'grace' show a thankful, respectful attitude.
example.answer: Central idea: every vocation is a gift that helps society, and no work is small. Tone: grateful and respectful.

learn.reallife: Think of the dabbawalas of Mumbai, the farmers who grow your rice and the nurses in hospitals: every vocation is a gift to everyone.

games.title: True or false about the poem
items: 'The teacher lights the minds awake' contains a metaphor.
The teacher is shown as someone who lights a lamp in the mind, an implied comparison.
Starting several lines with 'The' is an example of anaphora.
Anaphora is repeating the same word at the beginning of nearby lines.
The tone of a poem means the number of lines in it.
Tone is the poet's attitude or feeling, not the length.
'comfort, calm and care' is an example of alliteration.
The words repeat the same hard 'k' sound at the start.
A quatrain is a stanza of six lines.
The last two lines of the poem form a rhyming couplet.

quiz.q: 'No work is small, no hand is low; / Each gift of grace helps all to grow.' What is the central idea of these lines?
options: Some jobs are better than others
Every kind of work has value and helps everyone
quiz.explain: The lines say no work is small and every 'gift' of work helps all of us grow.
steps: The lines say no work is small and every gift helps all to grow.
So every kind of work has value.
Answer: Every kind of work has value and helps everyone
quiz.mistake: Reads 'small' and 'low' literally instead of as a judgement about work

quiz.q: 'Thank you, hands that sow the grain, / Thank you, hands that mend the drain.' What is the tone?
quiz.explain: The repeated 'Thank you' shows a grateful tone.
steps: Tone is shown by word choice.
The repeated 'Thank you' shows thankfulness.
Answer: Grateful
quiz.mistake: Ignores the words that reveal the poet's attitude

quiz.q: What is the repetition of the same word at the start of nearby lines called?
quiz.explain: Anaphora is repeating a word or phrase at the beginning of successive lines.
steps: Repeating a word or phrase at the start of nearby lines is anaphora.
Answer: Anaphora
quiz.mistake: Confuses repetition at the start with rhyme at the end

quiz.q: In the line 'No hand is low', what does 'hand' stand for?
quiz.explain: Here 'hand' stands for a person who works, as in 'farmhand'.
steps: 'Hand' here stands for a person who works, as in 'farmhand'.
Answer: A worker
quiz.mistake: Takes the word in its everyday literal sense

quiz.q: 'The weaver weaves the clothes we wear.' What is the subject of this sentence?
quiz.explain: The subject is who does the action: the weaver weaves.
steps: The subject is who does the action.
Who weaves? The weaver.
Answer: The weaver
quiz.mistake: Picks the object or the word nearest the verb

quiz.q: What does 'vocation' mean?
options: Work a person feels especially suited to
quiz.explain: A vocation is a job or calling that a person feels drawn to and suited for.
steps: A vocation is work a person feels suited to or called to do.
Answer: Work a person feels especially suited to
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'vocation' with 'vacation'

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'honour' when used as a verb?
quiz.explain: To honour someone is to respect them and show it.
steps: To honour someone is to respect them.
Answer: Respect
quiz.mistake: Picks an antonym

quiz.q: A stanza of two lines that usually rhyme is called a:
quiz.explain: A couplet is a pair of lines, usually rhyming.
steps: A pair of lines, usually rhyming, is a couplet.
A quatrain has four lines.
Answer: couplet
quiz.mistake: Mixes up couplet (two lines) and quatrain (four lines)

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: "What is this poem really saying, and how does the poet feel about workers?"
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! Every vocation is a gift, and the poet is full of gratitude. Thank you, farmers and weavers!
teach.nudge: Okay, but what is the main message, and what feeling does the poet show?

revise.summary: The poem honours different vocations and the gifts each brings to society. Readers find the central idea and tone, and recognise anaphora, couplets and quatrains.
remember: Central idea = the poem's main message in one or two sentences
Tone = the poet's attitude, e.g. grateful, joyful
Anaphora = repeating words at the start of nearby lines
Couplet = two lines; quatrain = four-line stanza
traps: Don't confuse tone with topic: the topic is work, the tone is grateful.
'Hand' in 'no hand is low' means a worker, not a body part.

chapters.title: Winds of Change (with poem: Canvas of Soil)

topics.title: Environment and change: words for a changing world

learn.hook: A pond full of plastic turns into a pond full of lotuses. What changed? People did!
points: The lesson 'Winds of Change' is an article about the Indian hand fan (pankha) and how its use has changed over time. Here we take its big idea, change, and learn words for our changing environment.

Key words: conserve (protect and use carefully), sustainable (meeting today's needs without harming the future), deforestation (cutting down forests), renewable (able to be replaced naturally, like solar and wind energy), biodegradable (able to be broken down naturally by tiny living things).
Word families: pollute, pollution, pollutant; environment, environmental, environmentalist; sustain, sustainable, sustainability.
The present perfect (has/have + past participle) describes a change whose result we see now: 'The lake has become cleaner.' It is not used with finished time words such as 'yesterday' or 'last year'.
Cause and effect are linked with connectors such as because, so, as a result and therefore. 'Although' shows contrast.

example.q: Read: 'Ten years ago the pond near Meena's school was choked with plastic. Then the students began a No-Plastic Tuesday drive. Now lotuses bloom there again and kingfishers have returned.' What caused the change, and which verb is in the present perfect?
steps: Find what happened just before the pond improved: the students' drive against plastic.
Look for has/have + past participle: 'have returned'.
example.answer: The students' No-Plastic Tuesday drive caused the change; 'have returned' is in the present perfect.

learn.reallife: Carrying a cloth bag to the market, using both sides of paper and switching off fans in an empty room are small changes that add up.

items.text: It rained heavily all night, ___ the river overflowed.
The air is smoky ___ of the fumes from the brick kiln.
We planted fifty trees; ___, the playground is cooler now.
___ he knew plastic was harmful, he still used plastic bags.

quiz.q: What does 'sustainable' mean?
options: Using things up as fast as possible
Meeting present needs without harming the future
quiz.explain: Sustainable living meets our needs today while protecting resources for the future.
steps: 'Sustainable' = meeting today's needs without harming the future.
Answer: Meeting present needs without harming the future
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'sustainable' just means 'strong' or 'lasting' for a short time

quiz.q: Which of these is biodegradable?
quiz.explain: A banana leaf is natural material that tiny organisms break down in a short time.
steps: Biodegradable = broken down naturally by tiny living things.
Plastic, glass and aluminium do not break down this way; a banana leaf does.
Answer: A banana-leaf plate
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything that can be thrown away is biodegradable

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the present perfect correctly?
options: Many birds have returned to the lake last winter.
Many birds has returned to the lake this winter.
Many birds have return to the lake this winter.
Many birds have returned to the lake this winter.
quiz.explain: 'Have returned' is have + past participle, and 'this winter' is a time that is not yet over.
steps: Present perfect = has/have + past participle, not with finished time words.
'last winter' is finished; 'has' does not agree with 'birds'; 'have return' lacks the participle.
Answer: Many birds have returned to the lake this winter.
quiz.mistake: Uses the present perfect with a finished time like 'last winter', or breaks agreement

quiz.q: What is the noun form of the verb 'pollute'?
quiz.explain: Adding -ion to 'pollute' gives the noun 'pollution'.
steps: The noun in the word family pollute → pollution → pollutant.
pollute + -ion = pollution
Answer: Pollution
quiz.mistake: Picks an -ed or -ing form, which are verb forms

quiz.q: What is the antonym of 'conserve'?
quiz.explain: To conserve is to use carefully; to waste is the opposite.
steps: Conserve = protect and use carefully.
Its opposite is to waste; protect, save, guard are synonyms.
Answer: Waste
quiz.mistake: Chooses a synonym instead of an antonym

quiz.q: Read: 'When the hills above the village lost their trees, the rains washed the soil down into the stream. The water turned muddy and the fields below flooded more often.' What made the stream muddy?
options: Soil washed down from the bare hills
quiz.explain: Without trees to hold it, the soil was washed into the stream by the rain.
steps: Cause: the hills lost their trees.
Effect: rain washed the soil into the stream, making it muddy.
Answer: Soil washed down from the bare hills
quiz.mistake: Brings in a cause that the passage does not mention

quiz.q: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
quiz.explain: The Sun's energy is replaced naturally every day, so it is renewable.
steps: Renewable = replaced naturally, like solar and wind energy.
Coal, petrol and kerosene are fossil fuels.
Answer: Solar energy
quiz.mistake: Thinks any common fuel is renewable

quiz.q: The phrase 'winds of change' is used to mean:
quiz.explain: 'Winds of change' is an expression for influences or forces that bring change.
steps: 'Winds of change' is an expression, not a real wind.
It means forces that bring new changes.
Answer: Forces that bring new changes
quiz.mistake: Takes the expression literally as wind

teach.ask: Gappu frowns: "The pond got cleaner. How do I say that in English, and what made it change?"
teach.praise: Chirp! 'The pond has become cleaner because people stopped throwing plastic.' Cause, effect and the present perfect!
teach.nudge: But what caused the change, and which tense shows a change we can see now?

revise.summary: 'Winds of Change' traces how the Indian hand fan's use changed over time. From its idea of change, we learn environment words, word families, the present perfect for changes we see now, and cause-effect connectors.
focus: Present perfect vs finished past time
Cause and effect in short passages
remember: Sustainable = meets today's needs without harming the future
Renewable = replaced naturally (solar, wind); biodegradable = broken down naturally
Present perfect = has/have + past participle (The lake has become cleaner.)
Cause-effect connectors: because, so, as a result, therefore; 'although' shows contrast
traps: Don't use the present perfect with 'last year' or 'yesterday'.
'Winds of change' is an expression, not a storm.

topics.title: Farming and soil: words from the field

learn.hook: Did you know a handful of healthy soil is home to millions of tiny living things? The soil is alive!
points: Farming words: sow (put seeds in the ground), irrigate (supply water to crops), harvest or reap (gather the ripe crop), fertile (able to grow good crops), barren (unable to grow crops), compost (rotted plant and food waste used to feed soil).
Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning: sow/sew, flour/flower, plain/plane, weather/whether.
In India, kharif crops such as rice, maize and cotton are sown with the start of the monsoon; rabi crops such as wheat, mustard and gram are sown in winter and harvested in spring.
Earthworms are called farmers' friends because they loosen the soil, let air and water in, and enrich it with their castings.
Alluvial soil, laid down by rivers, makes the northern plains very fertile; black soil holds moisture well and is especially good for cotton.

example.q: Fill the homophones: 'Baba will ___ the seeds, and Ma will ___ the torn sack.'
steps: The first blank is about seeds, so it needs the word meaning 'to plant': sow.
The second is about mending cloth with a needle: sew.
example.answer: sow, sew

learn.reallife: Festivals such as Baisakhi, Pongal and Bihu are linked with harvest time, when families thank the land for its crops.

games.title: Field words
pairs: Cut and gather the ripe crop
Able to grow plenty of crops
Rotted plant waste that feeds the soil

quiz.q: What is fertile soil?
options: Soil that can grow plenty of good crops
quiz.explain: Fertile soil is rich in nutrients and grows good crops.
steps: Fertile = able to grow good crops.
Answer: Soil that can grow plenty of good crops
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'fertile' with 'barren'

quiz.q: Which word is the antonym of 'fertile'?
quiz.explain: Barren land cannot grow crops, the opposite of fertile.
steps: The opposite of fertile is barren (unable to grow crops).
Rich, fruitful, productive are synonyms.
Answer: Barren
quiz.mistake: Chooses a synonym

quiz.q: Choose the correct homophone: 'Dadi ground the wheat into fine ___.'
quiz.explain: 'Flour' is powder made by grinding grain; a 'flower' is the bloom of a plant.
steps: Homophones flour/flower sound alike.
Ground wheat is flour; a flower is a bloom.
Answer: flour
quiz.mistake: Mixes up homophones that sound alike

quiz.q: Which of these is a rabi crop?
quiz.explain: Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in spring, so it is a rabi crop.
steps: Rabi crops (wheat, mustard, gram) are sown in winter.
Rice, cotton and maize are kharif crops.
Answer: Wheat
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the kharif and rabi seasons

quiz.q: Why are earthworms called farmers' friends?
options: They loosen the soil and make it richer
quiz.explain: Earthworms dig tunnels that let air and water in, and their castings add nutrients.
steps: Earthworms loosen the soil, let air and water in, and enrich it.
Answer: They loosen the soil and make it richer
quiz.mistake: Does not know how earthworms help soil

quiz.q: What does 'irrigate' mean?
options: To supply water to land or crops
quiz.explain: To irrigate is to bring water to fields, for example through canals, wells or drip pipes.
steps: Irrigate = supply water to crops.
Answer: To supply water to land or crops
quiz.mistake: Confuses irrigation with other farm jobs

quiz.q: Read: 'Kavya's grandfather never burns the leftover stalks after harvest. He ploughs them back into the field and spreads compost. "Feed the soil, and the soil will feed you," he says.' What does he mean?
options: Soil is a kind of food for people
Caring for the soil gives good crops in return
quiz.explain: He means that if we keep the soil healthy, it will give us good harvests.
steps: He returns stalks and compost to the soil.
His saying means healthy soil gives good harvests.
Answer: Caring for the soil gives good crops in return
quiz.mistake: Reads the saying literally

quiz.q: Which crop grows especially well in black soil?
quiz.explain: Black soil holds moisture well and is famous for cotton, which is why it is also called black cotton soil.
steps: Black soil holds moisture well.
It is especially good for cotton.
Answer: Cotton
quiz.mistake: Does not link black soil with cotton

teach.ask: Gappu scratches the ground: "Why do farmers care so much about soil? Teach me some field words!"
teach.praise: Wow! Fertile soil, sowing, harvesting and helpful earthworms. I'll never call soil 'just dirt' again!
teach.nudge: Hmm, what makes soil good for crops, and what do farmers do from seed to harvest?

revise.summary: This topic builds farming and soil vocabulary, homophones like sow/sew and flour/flower, and facts about kharif and rabi crops, earthworms and Indian soils.
remember: sow, irrigate, harvest/reap, fertile × barren, compost
Homophones: sow/sew, flour/flower, plain/plane, weather/whether
Kharif (monsoon): rice, maize, cotton; rabi (winter): wheat, mustard, gram
Alluvial soil makes the northern plains fertile; black soil suits cotton
traps: Wheat is a rabi crop, not kharif.
Don't confuse 'flour' (ground grain) with 'flower'.

topics.title: Canvas of Soil: metaphor and imagery in a farming poem

learn.hook: What if a field were a painting and the farmer were the painter? Poets love that kind of 'what if'!
points: The poem's title, 'Canvas of Soil', pictures the soil as a canvas, like a painter's.
An extended metaphor carries one comparison across several lines, for example field = canvas, plough = brush, crops = colours.
Imagery of colour, touch and smell helps the reader feel the field: green shoots, golden wheat, cool damp earth.
Degrees of comparison: positive (bright), comparative (brighter), superlative (brightest). Poets use them to make pictures vivid.
A good descriptive paragraph uses sensory details and precise adjectives instead of vague words like 'nice'.

example.q:
Read this original poem:
'The field is a canvas, bare and brown,
The plough, a brush, goes up and down;
With monsoon rain it paints in green,
The brightest shade you've ever seen.
In spring the wheat brings strokes of gold:
An artwork new, on earth so old.'
What is the extended metaphor here?
steps: Line 1 calls the field a canvas.
Line 2 calls the plough a brush.
Lines 3 to 6 talk of painting, shades, strokes and an artwork, so the painting comparison continues.
example.answer: Farming is shown as painting: the field is the canvas, the plough is the brush, and the crops are the colours.

learn.reallife: Look at a paddy field from a train window in the monsoon: the rows of bright green really do look like brushstrokes.

games.title: What does the image stand for?
pairs: Young crops after the monsoon rain

games.title: Build the sentence
games.prompt: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence

quiz.q: 'The field is a canvas, bare and brown.' What is the field compared to?
quiz.explain: The line directly says the field is a canvas, which is a metaphor.
steps: The line says the field IS a canvas.
That is a metaphor comparing it to a painter's canvas.
Answer: A canvas for painting
quiz.mistake: Picks another image from the poem

quiz.q: What is an extended metaphor?
options: A metaphor that is continued over several lines
A rhyme at the end of a line
quiz.explain: An extended metaphor develops one comparison through many lines or a whole poem.
steps: An extended metaphor carries one comparison across several lines.
Answer: A metaphor that is continued over several lines
quiz.mistake: Confuses an extended metaphor with a simile

quiz.q: In 'With monsoon rain it paints in green', what does the green stand for?
options: Green paint bought from a shop
Young crops growing after the rain
quiz.explain: After the monsoon rain, young crops cover the field in green.
steps: In the painting metaphor, crops are the colours.
After the monsoon rain, young crops turn the field green.
Answer: Young crops growing after the rain
quiz.mistake: Takes the painting image literally

quiz.q: What is the rhyme scheme of these lines? 'The field is a canvas, bare and brown, / The plough, a brush, goes up and down; / With monsoon rain it paints in green, / The brightest shade you've ever seen.'
quiz.explain: brown/down rhyme (aa) and green/seen rhyme (bb).
steps: Line endings: brown (a), down (a), green (b), seen (b).
Pattern: aabb.
Answer: aabb
quiz.mistake: Assigns letters without listening to the end sounds

quiz.q: Which phrase appeals to the sense of touch?
options: The cool, damp soil between my toes
quiz.explain: 'Cool' and 'damp' describe how something feels on the skin.
steps: Touch imagery describes how something feels on the skin.
'Cool, damp soil between my toes' is felt.
Answer: The cool, damp soil between my toes
quiz.mistake: Confuses sight, sound or taste imagery with touch

quiz.q: 'An artwork new, on earth so old.' What attitude does the poet show towards farming?
quiz.explain: Calling farming an 'artwork' shows that the poet admires it.
steps: Calling farming 'an artwork' praises it.
So the poet's attitude is admiration.
Answer: Admiration
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the positive word 'artwork'

quiz.q: In 'The brightest shade you've ever seen', which degree of comparison is 'brightest'?
quiz.explain: 'Brightest' (-est) compares one thing with all others, so it is superlative.
steps: Positive bright → comparative brighter → superlative brightest.
Answer: Superlative
quiz.mistake: Mixes up comparative (-er) and superlative (-est)

quiz.q: Which sentence is the most vivid description of a field?
options: The field was good and big.
Rows of tender green paddy shivered in the wet breeze.
quiz.explain: It uses precise adjectives and sensory details (tender, green, shivered, wet breeze).
steps: Vivid writing uses sensory details and precise adjectives.
'tender green paddy shivered in the wet breeze' does this; 'nice' and 'good' are vague.
Answer: Rows of tender green paddy shivered in the wet breeze.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a short, vague sentence is enough for description

teach.ask: Gappu looks puzzled: "How can a field be a canvas? Fields don't hang on walls!"
teach.praise: Tweet! It's an extended metaphor: the field is the canvas, the plough the brush, and the crops are the colours!
teach.nudge: But what is being compared to what? Which farm things are the canvas, the brush and the colours?

revise.summary: 'Canvas of Soil' pictures the field as a painter's canvas, an extended metaphor in which the plough is a brush and crops are colours. Sensory imagery and degrees of comparison make the description vivid.
focus: Degrees of comparison and vivid description
remember: Extended metaphor = one comparison carried across several lines
Field = canvas, plough = brush, crops = colours
Positive bright, comparative brighter, superlative brightest
Use sensory details and precise adjectives, not vague words like 'nice'
traps: The green in the poem is crops, not paint.
A single comparison is a metaphor; continued across lines it is an extended metaphor.

chapters.title: Vitamin-M (with poem: I Cannot Remember My Mother)

topics.title: Family and mothers: words of love and care

learn.hook: Who remembers to pack your tiffin, even on the busiest morning? Families speak love in a hundred quiet ways.
points: The lesson 'Vitamin-M' is a family story about a boy, Ravi, and his grandfather, whose memory has grown weak. It shows that elders need patience, care and respect from their family, and its paired poem by Tagore remembers a mother.
Words of care: nurture (care for and help to grow), affection (fondness, gentle love), devotion (deep loyalty and love), cherish (hold dear), sacrifice (give up something for someone else).

Family phrasal verbs: bring up (raise a child), look after (take care of), take after (resemble an older family member), get along with (have a friendly relationship), look up to (admire and respect).
Idioms: 'the apple of someone's eye' means a person who is very dear; 'runs in the family' means a quality shared by many family members.
Writers often show love through actions rather than words. Readers infer feelings from what characters do.

example.q: Read: 'Amma's alarm rings at five. By the time Ishaan wakes up, his tiffin is packed, his uniform ironed and a glass of warm haldi milk waits on the table. Amma only says, "Drink it before it gets cold." Ishaan smiles; he knows that is her way of saying "I love you."' How does Amma show her love?
steps: Look at what Amma does: wakes early, packs the tiffin, irons the uniform, warms milk.
Look at what she says: only a simple reminder.
Ishaan's thought tells us her actions carry the message of love.
example.answer: She shows her love through caring actions rather than many words.

learn.reallife: Next time someone in your family keeps the last piece of mithai for you, you'll know it is love in action!

items.text: Riya is the ___ of her grandfather's eye.
Musical talent runs in the ___; her mother and aunt both sing.
Aarav really takes ___ his father; they have the same smile.
My aunt brought ___ three children while working full-time.

quiz.q: What does 'nurture' mean?
options: To care for and help to grow
quiz.explain: To nurture is to look after someone or something and help it develop.
steps: 'Nurture' = care for and help to grow.
Answer: To care for and help to grow
quiz.mistake: Does not know the word and guesses a negative meaning

quiz.q: What does 'look after' mean in 'Didi looks after our baby brother'?
quiz.explain: 'Look after' means to take care of someone.
steps: 'Look after' = take care of.
Answer: Takes care of
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'look after' with 'look for' or 'take after'

quiz.q: 'Meera looks up to her mother.' What does this mean?
options: Meera is taller than her mother
Meera admires and respects her mother
quiz.explain: To look up to someone is to admire and respect them.
steps: 'Look up to' = admire and respect.
Answer: Meera admires and respects her mother

topics.title: Talking in the family: reported speech

learn.hook: Your little brother runs to you: 'Ma said you have to come home now!' He has just used reported speech!
points: Direct speech gives the exact words in quotation marks: Ma said, "I am tired." Reported (indirect) speech gives the meaning without quotation marks: Ma said that she was tired.
When the reporting verb is in the past, tenses usually move one step back: am/is → was, are → were, will → would, can → could, present perfect → past perfect.
Pronouns and time or place words change: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, now → then, here → there. 'Said to' becomes 'told'.
Questions: yes/no questions use 'asked if/whether'; wh-questions keep the wh-word but use normal word order (asked where I was going).
Commands and requests use told/asked/requested + object + to + verb; a negative command uses 'not to'.

example.q: Change into reported speech: Ma said to me, "I am making kheer today."
steps: 'said to me' becomes 'told me'.
'I' (Ma) becomes 'she'; 'am making' moves back to 'was making'.
'today' becomes 'that day'.
example.answer: Ma told me that she was making kheer that day.

topics.title: Tagore's poem on memory: senses and feelings

learn.hook: Can a smell bring back a person? Catch a whiff of jasmine and suddenly you are in Nani's courtyard again!
points: Rabindranath Tagore (1861-1941) was a poet, writer, composer and painter from Bengal. In 1913 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature and became the first Asian to win a Nobel Prize.
Tagore wrote 'Jana Gana Mana', India's national anthem, and founded Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan.
In his poem 'I Cannot Remember My Mother', the speaker cannot clearly recall his mother, yet feels her presence in everyday sounds, scents and sights.
Memory poems often use sensory imagery and a nostalgic tone. Nostalgia is a warm, slightly sad longing for the past.
'Used to' + verb describes a past habit that no longer happens: 'Nani used to sing while she cooked.'

example.q:
Read this original poem:
'I cannot see Nani's face so clear,
Yet when the evening kettle sings
Or jasmine scent drifts softly near,
I feel her close in little things.
Her lullabies still hum in rain;
She's far, yet always comes again.'
Which senses bring back the memory, and what is the tone?
steps: 'the evening kettle sings' and 'lullabies' are sounds: hearing.
'jasmine scent' is a smell.
The speaker misses Nani but feels comforted, so the tone is tender and nostalgic.
example.answer: Hearing and smell bring back the memory; the tone is tender and nostalgic.

learn.reallife: The smell of a particular agarbatti, the tune of an old film song or the taste of a festival sweet can bring back a loved one in a flash.

topics.title: Sports and inclusion: words that open doors

learn.hook: What makes a game truly great: the fastest player, or the moment when everyone gets to play?
points: The lesson 'The World of Limitless Possibilities' is linked with sport and inclusion: people of all abilities taking part.

Key words: inclusion (making sure everyone is welcomed and can take part), accessible (easy for everyone, including people with disabilities, to reach and use), empathy (understanding and sharing another person's feelings), perseverance (continuing despite difficulty), resilience (the ability to bounce back).
Respectful, people-first language puts the person before the condition: 'a person with a disability', 'an athlete who uses a wheelchair'.
Prefixes make opposites: include/exclude, fair/unfair, able/unable, possible/impossible, accessible/inaccessible.
Adjectives describe nouns (a quick runner); adverbs usually describe verbs (she ran quickly). Many adverbs end in -ly.

example.q: Read: 'When the class planned sports day, Kabir, who uses a wheelchair, expected to sit and watch. But his classmates added a wheelchair relay and a seated ball-throw. That evening Kabir wore a medal and the widest grin on the school bus.' How did the classmates show inclusion?
steps: Notice Kabir's expectation: he thought he would only watch.
Notice what the classmates changed: they added events he could take part in.
The result: he took part and won a medal.
example.answer: They changed the events so that Kabir could take part, instead of leaving him out.

learn.reallife: Ramps beside steps, audio announcements at railway stations and Braille on lift buttons all make places accessible.

topics.title: The Special Olympics spirit

learn.hook: Imagine a sports meet where the loudest cheer is not for the fastest runner, but for the bravest try!
points: Special Olympics is a worldwide sports movement for people with intellectual disabilities. It was started by Eunice Kennedy Shriver, and the first International Special Olympics Summer Games were held in Chicago, USA, in 1968.
Its athlete oath is: 'Let me win. But if I cannot win, let me be brave in the attempt.' It values courage and effort over medals alone.
Athletes are grouped with others of similar ability so that every race is fair and everyone has a real chance. In India the movement is run by Special Olympics Bharat.
Unified Sports brings people with and without intellectual disabilities together as teammates.
Sports collocations are words that naturally go together: take part, break a record, win a medal, cross the finish line, cheer on.

example.q: Think it through: What does 'let me be brave in the attempt' mean in the athlete oath?
steps: 'Attempt' means a try or an effort.

So it asks for courage while trying, whatever the result.
example.answer: It means that even if I don't win, I want to try with courage and give my best effort.

learn.reallife: Many Indian schools hold inclusive sports days and Unified Sports matches where children of all abilities play on the same team.

topics.title: Nine Gold Medals: a story told in a poem

learn.hook: A poem that tells a whole story, with a twist at the end? That's a narrative poem, and you're about to read one!
points: 'Nine Gold Medals' is a narrative poem about athletes in a race who choose kindness over winning.
A narrative poem tells a story with characters, a setting, events, a climax (the turning point) and an ending.
A paradox is a statement that seems to contradict itself but holds a deeper truth, for example 'We lost, yet we won'.
Stories in verse usually use the simple past: ran, fell, knelt, cheered.
A good summary gives only the main events in your own words and in the right order, and is much shorter than the original.

example.q:
Read this original narrative poem:
'Our team was one point from the cup
When Meenu's shoelace tangled up;
The rival captain paused the play
And knelt to help her on her way.
We lost the match, the scoreboard said,
But all of us walked home ahead.'
What is the climax, and what is the message?
steps: The tension builds: the team is one point from winning.
The turning point is when the rival captain stops the play to help Meenu.
The last two lines say they lost on the scoreboard but felt like winners.
example.answer: The climax is the rival captain pausing the play to help Meenu. The message: kindness and sportsmanship matter more than the score.

learn.reallife: Think of a time a player in a cricket or football match helped an injured opponent; the crowd often claps more for that than for a goal.

learn.hook: A tabla, a flute and a power cut: that's all it takes to turn a dark corridor into a concert!
points: The lesson 'Twin Melodies' is a play about Shruti, a young violinist who plays fusion music with her band, and her father, who loves traditional music. Music is at its heart, and the paired poem shows music as a friend.
Music words: melody (a tune), rhythm (a pattern of beats), tempo (the speed of music), lyrics (the words of a song), harmony (different notes sounding pleasant together).
Indian classical music has two main traditions: Hindustani, mainly in North India, and Carnatic, mainly in South India. A raga is a melodic framework; a tala is a rhythmic cycle.
Instruments can be grouped as string (sitar, veena, sarod), wind (bansuri, shehnai, nadaswaram) and percussion (tabla, mridangam, dholak).

Great Indian musicians: Ustad Bismillah Khan (shehnai), Pandit Ravi Shankar (sitar), Ustad Zakir Hussain (tabla), Pandit Hariprasad Chaurasia (bansuri) and M. S. Subbulakshmi (Carnatic vocal), the first musician to receive the Bharat Ratna.

topics.title: Friendship: idioms, phrasal verbs and relative clauses

learn.hook: Who is the friend you'd call first with good news? Friendship has its own special vocabulary!
points: Friendship words: companion (someone you spend time with), confidant (a person you trust with secrets), loyal (faithful), trustworthy (can be relied on), inseparable (always together).
Phrasal verbs: stand by (support), count on (rely on), fall out (quarrel), make up (become friends again after a quarrel), drift apart (slowly become less close).

Idioms: 'a friend in need is a friend indeed' (a true friend helps when you need it), 'thick as thieves' (very close), 'see eye to eye' (agree), 'break the ice' (start a friendly conversation in an awkward moment).
Relative pronouns join ideas: who for people (a friend who listens), which for things (the song which we sang), whose for possession (the boy whose sister sings).

topics.title: A Friend Found in Music: sound devices in poetry

learn.hook: Have you ever felt that a song understood you better than anyone? Poets call that a friendship too!
points: The poem in this lesson presents music as a companion that comforts and stays with us.

Sound devices make poems musical: rhyme (matching end sounds), rhythm (a pattern of beats), alliteration (repeated beginning consonant sounds), assonance (repeated vowel sounds inside nearby words, as in 'sweet green leaves') and onomatopoeia (words that imitate sounds, like jingle or dhum).
A refrain is a line or group of lines repeated in a poem or song, like a chorus.
Personification lets music act like a person: it can whisper, hug or hold your hand.
'Feeling blue' is an idiom meaning feeling sad.

example.q:

The flute-notes whisper, "Don't be blue,"

A friend that lifts my dancing feet.'

steps: Music 'comes', 'taps my shoulder' and the flute-notes 'whisper': these are human actions.
'Dha-dhin' imitates the sound of the tabla.
example.answer: Personification: 'music comes / And taps my shoulder' (also 'flute-notes whisper'). Onomatopoeia: 'Dha-dhin'.

topics.title: Communication: getting the message across

learn.hook: A wink, a postcard, a voice note and a namaste: four very different ways to say something!
points: The lesson 'Carrier of Words' is about communication, that is, how messages travel from one person to another.
Verbal communication uses words, spoken or written. Non-verbal communication uses gestures, facial expressions, body language and tone of voice.
Formal language suits officials and people we don't know well: full sentences, polite requests, no slang. Informal language suits friends and family and may use contractions like I'm and can't.
A formal letter has: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation (Sir/Madam), body, complimentary close (Yours faithfully), and signature with name.
In India, the six-digit PIN code (Postal Index Number) helps the postal service deliver letters to the right area.

Line (b) is a polite, complete request using formal words like 'request' and 'kindly grant'.

topics.title: The power of words: shades of meaning

learn.hook: 'Slim' or 'skinny'? 'Curious' or 'nosy'? One small word choice can make someone smile or frown!
points: Words can hurt or heal, so we choose them with care. 'Think before you speak' is good advice.
Denotation is a word's dictionary meaning. Connotation is the feeling a word carries: 'thrifty' sounds positive, 'stingy' sounds negative, though both describe careful spending.
Polite words and phrases (please, could you, thank you, I'm sorry) make requests and disagreements kinder.
Tricky homophones: its (belonging to it) / it's (it is); your (belonging to you) / you're (you are); their (belonging to them) / there (a place) / they're (they are).
The saying 'The pen is mightier than the sword' means ideas and words can have more power than force.

example.q: Which feedback on a friend's drawing is kinder and more useful? (a) 'Your drawing is bad.' (b) 'I love the colours; maybe the trees could be a little bigger?'

(b) praises something real and gives a gentle, specific suggestion.
example.answer: (b), because it is kind and gives a clear suggestion for improvement.

topics.title: Words: a poem about words, and parts of speech

learn.hook: A single word can be a noun at breakfast and a verb by lunch. Words are shape-shifters!
points: The poem 'Words' in this lesson is about the power of words.
Metaphors help poets show the power of words: words as seeds, thorns or wings.
English has eight parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection.
The same word can be a different part of speech in different sentences: 'Switch on the light' (noun), 'Light the diya' (verb), 'a light bag' (adjective).
Conjunctions (and, but, because) join words or clauses; prepositions (in, on, under) show how a noun relates to other words; interjections (Wow! Oh!) express sudden feeling.

example.q:
Read this original poem:
'Words are seeds we gently sow,
In other hearts they root and grow;
A harsh word is a thorn that stings,
A kind word gives the spirit wings.
So weigh each word before it flies:
Once spoken, no word ever dies.'
What is the poem's message, and name one metaphor.
steps: Lines 1 to 4 show words growing in hearts, stinging or lifting people.
Lines 5 and 6 advise us to think before we speak because words last.
'Words are seeds' says words ARE seeds, without 'like' or 'as'.
example.answer: Message: words have lasting power, so think before you speak. Metaphor: 'Words are seeds' (also 'A harsh word is a thorn').

learn.reallife: A kind message to a friend before an exam can stay with them for years; so can a mean comment. That's why we weigh our words.

'Light' can be a noun, a verb or an adjective, depending on the sentence.

An interjection expresses a sudden feeling, like 'Oh!' or 'Hurray!'

chapters.title: Follow That Dream (with poem: Believe in Yourself)

topics.title: Ambition: dreams, goals and talking about the future

learn.hook: Every big dream starts as a tiny 'what if'. What if you are the next great scientist, singer or athlete?
points: The lesson 'Follow That Dream' is about ambition: having a goal and working steadily towards it.

Key words: ambition (a strong wish to achieve something), aspire (to hope and work to achieve something), goal, obstacle (something in the way), persevere (keep going despite difficulty), milestone (an important stage of progress).
Talking about the future: 'will' for predictions and on-the-spot decisions; 'be going to' for plans and for things we can see coming ('Look at those clouds; it is going to rain').
The present continuous can show fixed arrangements ('I am meeting my coach tomorrow'); the simple present is used for timetables ('The train leaves at 6:10').
Big dreams become real through small, steady steps.

example.q: Choose the right future form: 'Look at those dark clouds! It ___ rain.'
steps: We can see evidence now: dark clouds.
When present evidence shows something is about to happen, we use 'be going to'.

learn.reallife: Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam grew up in Rameswaram and sold newspapers as a boy before becoming a scientist and President of India. Kalpana Chawla became the first woman of Indian origin to go to space.

topics.title: Self-belief: idioms and contrast words

learn.hook: What do you say to yourself just before an exam? Those quiet words might be the most important ones of the day!
points: Self-belief is confidence in your own abilities. Self-doubt is its opposite. An optimistic person expects good things; a pessimistic person expects the worst.
Idioms: 'keep your chin up' (stay cheerful in hard times), 'rise to the occasion' (do well when it really matters), 'never say die' (never give up), 'against all odds' (despite great difficulties).
Positive self-talk turns 'I can't do this' into 'I can't do this yet, but I'm learning.'

Contrast words: 'although' and 'even though' are followed by a clause (Although she was nervous, she sang). 'Despite' and 'in spite of' are followed by a noun or an -ing form (Despite her nerves, she sang). We never say 'despite of'.

example.q: Join the two sentences using 'although': 'She was nervous. She sang beautifully.'
steps: 'Although' introduces the contrasting idea, which has a subject and a verb: she was nervous.
Add a comma, then the main clause.
example.answer: Although she was nervous, she sang beautifully.

learn.reallife: Before a match, a speech or a board exam, many people take a deep breath and remind themselves how much they have prepared.

It encourages someone not to lose hope.

topics.title: Believe in Yourself: imperatives, sentence types and diary writing

learn.hook: 'Stand up! Try again! Believe!' Notice anything? Poems of courage love command words!
points: The poem 'Believe in Yourself' in this lesson encourages the reader to trust their own strength and keep going.
Imperative sentences give commands, advice or encouragement. They start with the base form of a verb, and the subject 'you' is understood: 'Stand firm.'
The four types of sentences are declarative (statement), interrogative (question), imperative (command or request) and exclamatory (strong feeling, often with What or How and an exclamation mark).
Repeating a word at the start of lines (anaphora) and making storms or doubts speak (personification) add force to a poem.
A diary entry has the date, day and time, is written in the first person, records events and feelings in an informal style, and ends with your name.

example.q:
Read this original poem:
'Believe the seed that dreams of tree,
Believe the stream that seeks the sea;
When storms say "Stop!" and doubts say "No,"
Stand up, stand firm, and still say "Go!"
The sky is not your ceiling, friend:
It's just the start, it's not the end.'
Find an imperative and explain 'The sky is not your ceiling'.
steps: 'Stand up, stand firm' begins with base verbs and gives encouragement: imperative.
A ceiling stops you from going higher; the poet says the sky is not such a limit.
So the line means there is no fixed limit to how far you can rise.
example.answer: Imperative: 'Stand up, stand firm'. 'The sky is not your ceiling' means there is no limit to what you can achieve.

learn.reallife: Keeping a diary of your goals and small wins, like finishing a chapter or a tough practice session, is a great way to build self-belief.
